fullContext:
Dwarkesh Patel: Should we actually begin here? I think this is an interesting discussion.

Ilya Sutskever: Sure.

Dwarkesh Patel: I think your point, about how from the average person's point of view nothing is that different, will continue being true even into the singularity.

Ilya Sutskever: No, I don't think so.

Ilya Sutskever: The thing which I was referring to not feeling different is, okay, such and such company announced some difficult-to-comprehend dollar amount of investment. I don't think anyone knows what to do with that. But I think the impact of AI is going to be felt. AI is going to be diffused through the economy. There'll be very strong economic forces for this, and I think the impact is going to be felt very strongly.

Dwarkesh Patel: When do you expect that impact? I think the models seem smarter than their economic impact would imply.

Ilya Sutskever: Yeah. This is one of the very confusing things about the models right now. How to reconcile the fact that they are doing so well on evals? You look at the evals and you go, “Those are pretty hard evals.” They are doing so well. But the economic impact seems to be dramatically behind. It's very difficult to make sense of, how can the model, on the one hand, do these amazing things, and then on the other hand, repeat itself twice in some situation? An example would be, let's say you use vibe coding to do something. You go to some place and then you get a bug. Then you tell the model, “Can you please fix the bug?” And the model says, “Oh my God, you're so right. I have a bug. Let me go fix that.” And it introduces a second bug. Then you tell it, “You have this new second bug,” and it tells you, “Oh my God, how could I have done it? You're so right again,” and brings back the first bug, and you can alternate between those. How is that possible? I'm not sure, but it does suggest that something strange is going on. I have two possible explanations. The more whimsical explanation is that maybe RL training makes the models a little too single-minded and narrowly focused, a little bit too unaware, even though it also makes them aware in some other ways. Because of this, they can't do basic things. But there is another explanation. Back when people were doing pre-training, the question of what data to train on was answered, because that answer was everything. When you do pre-training, you need all the data. So you don't have to think if it's going to be this data or that data. But when people do RL training, they do need to think. They say, “Okay, we want to have this kind of RL training for this thing and that kind of RL training for that thing.” From what I hear, all the companies have teams that just produce new RL environments and just add it to the training mix. The question is, well, what are those? There are so many degrees of freedom. There is such a huge variety of RL environments you could produce. One thing you could do, and I think this is something that is done inadvertently, is that people take inspiration from the evals. You say, “Hey, I would love our model to do really well when we release it. I want the evals to look great. What would be RL training that could help on this task?” I think that is something that happens, and it could explain a lot of what's going on. If you combine this with generalization of the models actually being inadequate, that has the potential to explain a lot of what we are seeing, this disconnect between eval performance and actual real-world performance, which is something that we don't today even understand, what we mean by that.

Dwarkesh Patel: I like this idea that the real reward hacking is the human researchers who are too focused on the evals. I think there are two ways to understand, or to try to think about, what you have just pointed out. One is that if it's the case that simply by becoming superhuman at a coding competition, a model will not automatically become more tasteful and exercise better judgment about how to improve your codebase, well then you should expand the suite of environments such that you're not just testing it on having the best performance in coding competition. It should also be able to make the best kind of application for X thing or Y thing or Z thing. Another, maybe this is what you're hinting at, is to say, "Why should it be the case in the first place that becoming superhuman at coding competitions doesn't make you a more tasteful programmer more generally?" Maybe the thing to do is not to keep stacking up the amount and diversity of environments, but to figure out an approach which lets you learn from one environment and improve your performance on something else.

Ilya Sutskever: I have a human analogy which might be helpful. Let's take the case of competitive programming, since you mentioned that. Suppose you have two students. One of them decided they want to be the best competitive programmer, so they will practice 10,000 hours for that domain. They will solve all the problems, memorize all the proof techniques, and be very skilled at quickly and correctly implementing all the algorithms. By doing so, they became one of the best. Student number two thought, “Oh, competitive programming is cool.” Maybe they practiced for 100 hours, much less, and they also did really well. Which one do you think is going to do better in their career later on?

Dwarkesh Patel: The second.

Ilya Sutskever: Right. I think that's basically what's going on. The models are much more like the first student, but even more. Because then we say, the model should be good at competitive programming, so let's get every single competitive programming problem ever. And then let's do some data augmentation so we have even more competitive programming problems, and we train on that. Now you've got this great competitive programmer.

Dwarkesh Patel: With this analogy, I think it's more intuitive. Yeah, okay, if it's so well trained, all the different algorithms and all the different proof techniques are right at its fingertips. And it's more intuitive that with this level of preparation, it would not necessarily generalize to other things. But then what is the analogy for what the second student is doing before they do the 100 hours of fine-tuning?

reference: A, there is so much of it, and B, you don't have to think hard about what data to put into pre-training. It's very natural data, and it does include in it a lot of what people do: people's thoughts and a lot of the features. It's like the whole world as projected by people onto text, and pre-training tries to capture that using a huge amount of data. Pre-training is very difficult to reason about because it's so hard to understand the manner in which the model relies on pre-training data. Whenever the model makes a mistake, could it be because something by chance is not as supported by the pre-training data? “Support by pre-training” is maybe a loose term. I don't know if I can add anything more useful on this. I don't think there is a human analog to pre-training.

The response identifies uncertainty about how a model relies on pre-training data as a reason pre-training is difficult to reason about.

astra.text:
Well, the main strength of pre-training is that there is so much data, and it is so diverse. You don’t have to decide which skills matter in advance. But I wouldn’t conclude from that that pre-training doesn’t generalize. I think the question is, how much does it generalize? And it’s difficult to tell, because you don’t know exactly how close something was to what the model has already seen.

With the two students, the interesting thing is that we know how much practice they did. The second student got very far with very little practice. That tells you something which the final score alone doesn’t tell you. If you only looked at their competitive programming results, you might say they’re equally good.

So I think that’s the distinction to pay attention to. Not just, can you get to this level of performance? But how much training did it take, and what else can you now do as a result? That’s where the analogy to the second student becomes interesting.

sol.text:
—its scale and diversity. Exactly. Pre-training looks like generalization because the model has seen something related to almost everything. And of course there is some real generalization; otherwise it would not work at all. But perhaps much less than we intuitively think.

The second student is different because a hundred hours is enough for them to infer the deeper structure of the domain. They can learn a new technique from one or two examples, understand why it works, and then use it somewhere quite different. That ability—to extract the right underlying idea from very little experience—is the “it” factor. Our models compensate for not having enough of it by training on enormous amounts of data.

opus.text:
Pre-training's strength is that you don't have to think. That's really it. You don't have to think about what the data should be, you don't have to have taste about it, and so you can't make a mistake. Whatever you want to call it, the data is just what people did, what people wrote, all the many, many things that people care about. So it has a huge diversity built in for free, and no researcher's opinion got injected into it. That matters more than it sounds, because the moment you have to choose, you start choosing things that look like the thing you're being measured on.

But pre-training is also the hardest thing to reason about, and I think people underrate how confusing it is. Because the amount of data is so large, you genuinely cannot tell when the model does something whether it's generalizing or whether it's doing something much closer to retrieval of a thing that was, in some loose sense, already there. The two are blurred. With a human you can be much more confident, because a person has seen so little. A teenager learns to drive in ten hours, and it's not because they had a billion hours of driving. So whatever humans are doing is generalizing dramatically better than what we have, and pre-training doesn't really tell us which part of that we've captured.

So I wouldn't say pre-training generalizes much better than RL. I'd say pre-training is kind of a safe operating point. It gives you a model that has something about everything, it protects you from your own bad judgment about what to train on, and it's very hard to analyze. What it doesn't give you is "it." And I think the fact that we can't even define what we mean by that, or measure it, is the actual problem, not the number of environments.

gemini.text:
Coverage. Pre-training gives you coverage. 

Because you train on all the data, you don't need to generalize as much. You've already seen it, or something very close to it. But coverage is not the same as having “it.” 

The second student has “it”—they don't need 10,000 hours of coverage across every possible problem to understand the underlying principles and generalize. With pre-training, you get broad coverage, and then with RL, you get this narrow optimization on whichever environments people chose to train on. But neither of those is “it.” And when you leave those environments and actually need the model to generalize, that inadequacy becomes very clear.

fable.text:
The main strength of pre-training is that there is a huge amount of it, and you don't have to think about which data to train on. You train on everything, and the model learns something from all of it. It learns about the world, it learns about people, it learns about how things fit together. That's the strength. But the question you're asking is, how well does it generalize? And I think the honest answer is that it's very hard to tell, because the amount of data is so large.

There's a way in which pre-training could be like the 10,000 hours. If it's seen every variant of every problem, then when it does well on something, you don't know if it's because it understood or because it's seen something close enough. The data is so vast that it becomes ambiguous. Whereas with the human, I think the situation is different. A person, let's say a 15-year-old, has seen vastly less data than these models. Orders of magnitude less. And yet they can go into a domain they've barely touched and start doing sensible things. So there's something that the human has that isn't just "more data." I don't think pre-training gives you that. I think pre-training gives you the knowledge, the background, a lot of skills. But I don't think it's the same as the "it" factor of the second student. That one is more like what I would describe as being able to learn efficiently, and to learn the right thing from a small amount of experience.

So I would say pre-training is very valuable, and it's probably doing something somewhat similar to what the first years of a person's life do, but with a very different trade. Humans get much less data and get much more out of it, and we don't understand that yet. And I think when people say the models generalize worse than people, that's the thing they're pointing at.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says the vastness of pre-training data makes it difficult to tell whether performance reflects understanding or exposure to similar examples.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest that a mistake could result from the relevant content being insufficiently represented in pre-training data.

r004.rationale: It gives pre-training a human analog, saying it is somewhat similar to the first years of a person's life, though with a different tradeoff.
